15.t: Working with data: diet and coat colour
q: Describe the relationship between promoter methylation and coat colour.
More methylation, more brown, lean offspring and fewer yellow ones (8%: 15% brown; 35%: 50% brown).
Explain how methylation of the promoter affects the agouti gene.
Methyl groups on cytosines in the promoter stop transcription factors and RNA polymerase binding, so the gene is silenced: less agouti protein, brown coat and normal weight.
Explain why the mothers had to be genetically identical.
So that differences between the offspring are caused by the diet (environment), not by different alleles.
Evaluate the claim that methyl donors can cancel out the effect of BPA.
Supported: with donors, methylation rose from 8% to 25% and brown offspring from 15% to 35%. But this is one mouse study, so we cannot assume the same in humans.
Suggest why results like these matter for human health.
A mother’s diet or chemical exposure in pregnancy could change gene expression in her children, with lasting effects such as obesity.

20.t: Working with data: methylation in twins
q: Describe the trend for twins living together.
The difference increases with age, from 1.0 at 3 to 4.8 at 50, and rises faster in adults.
Calculate the mean increase per year between 28 and 50 for twins living together.
Twins living apart differ more at the same age. Explain.
They meet different environments (diet, smoking, stress, illness), which change methylation in different ways.
Explain why identical twins are useful for studying epigenetics.
They have the same DNA base sequence, so any differences in methylation must come from the environment or chance.
Suggest why the difference is not zero even at age 3.
Methylation patterns are not copied perfectly at every division (random errors), and twins can have slightly different conditions in the womb.
